title: Automation Could Shrink US Labor Demand by 36 Million Jobs by 2035, McKinsey Warns
excerpt: The McKinsey Global Institute says 11 million US workers — 7% of the workforce — may need entirely new occupations as AI adoption accelerates, in "the largest workforce transformation in US history."
body:
• A new McKinsey Global Institute report predicts automation could cut US labor demand equivalent to 36 million jobs — 21% of current work hours — by 2035.
  • About 11 million workers, or roughly 7% of the US workforce, may need to switch occupations entirely; 770,000 would have to make that move every year, 3.6 times the historical average.
  • The hardest-hit fields are office and administrative support, agriculture, technology and analytics, manufacturing, and retail and sales — but even those who stay will face change: more than 70% of workers will need "some level of reinvention."
  • For Indian tech workers and H-1B holders in the US: healthcare, construction and management roles are projected to grow fastest, and only one in seven displaced workers has a direct route into a growing field with limited retraining — reskilling now is the hedge.

The numbers that frame the decade

The McKinsey Global Institute's base estimate is stark: by 2035, automation technologies could absorb about 54% of current US work hours. After offsetting effects — productivity gains, new tasks, regulation — the net reduction in labor demand is equal to about 21% of current hours, or 36 million jobs. That is the headline number. The more human one is this: roughly 25 million of the affected workers should be able to stay in their current occupations because industry growth offsets automation, but about 11 million will need to switch occupations entirely, with the range running from 6 million to 16 million depending on how fast automation is adopted.

The transition is heavily lopsided by wage. Lower-wage workers are 7.6 times more likely than higher-wage workers to need to change occupations. And moving is no simple matter: only about one in seven displaced workers has a direct route into a growing occupation that requires limited retraining while offering at least comparable pay.

Which jobs disappear — and which grow

Automation adoption will not be evenly spread. McKinsey expects average adoption to reach roughly 80% of current hours in office and administrative support by 2035, 70% in technology and analytics, and 68% in retail and sales. By contrast, healthcare professionals come in at 26% and public safety and security at 28%. The occupations with the highest exposure include office and administrative support, agriculture, fishing and forestry, technology and analytics, manufacturing and production, and retail and sales, along with business and finance, food service, transportation and logistics, and installation and repair.

US Labor Department data sharpens the picture for the fastest-declining jobs: word processors and typists are projected to fall 34.4% by 2035, telephone operators 27.6%, and data entry keyers 25.5%. In raw numbers, cashiers top the losses at about 200,600 jobs, followed by office clerks (156,200), customer service representatives (141,800) and secretaries (114,100). On the growth side, healthcare, construction and management are expected to see stronger demand — nurse practitioner jobs alone are projected to grow 41% by 2035.

The counter-argument: demand, not scarcity

McKinsey's report is not a doomsday forecast. Its core line: "The next decade's challenge is mobility, not scarcity." The US economy is expected to add more than 40 million new jobs over the same period, and demand growth should exceed the decline. Tanguy Catlin, a director at the McKinsey Global Institute, told CNBC the transition will still be difficult for workers caught in it. The report draws a useful distinction: technology determines what is theoretically automatable, but managerial decisions determine how fast it happens — and four offsets (productivity-driven demand growth, new tasks like reviewing machine output, regulatory barriers, and relief for overworked staff) absorb about 60% of the raw automation effect.

"Technology determines what is possible, but managerial choices determine how quickly those possibilities become reality."

— McKinsey Global Institute

Diaspora angle

This report lands on a US labor market Indian workers already find unsettled — H-1B fee fights, green-card suspensions and entry-level hiring freezes. The McKinsey numbers add a structural layer to the cyclical one: technology and analytics, where Indian professionals are concentrated, faces 70% adoption of current hours by 2035. The actionable read: occupational mobility is the new job security. Workers in declining functions who retrain into adjacent growing fields — data-adjacent roles moving toward AI systems work, for example — are the ones with a direct route. Waiting for the displacement to arrive is the one move the report prices as the worst.

What's next

Whether the base case or the pessimistic one wins depends on adoption speed, which the report says is a management choice, not a technological inevitability. Watch employer reskilling programs, regulatory barriers and union agreements — they are the levers that decide whether the 11 million becomes 6 million or 16 million. For the underlying research, see CNN's summary and Fast Company.
